# The ISLA forward pass {#sec-architecture}

**This chapter states exactly what ISLA computes, stage by stage, with one
name for every quantity and the tensor shape beside it.** @sec-isla explains
why each part is there. This chapter is the reference for *what* the class
does, and the other chapters and the code are held to it. Read it with
@fig-isla-pass open. Every stage below is one box of that figure, and every
equation names the identifier that computes it in
`physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/model.py`. The description uses a
width $d$, a stack of 12 slice layers and $M$ slices; the class defaults
to 12 layers and 512 slices. Nothing in it depends on those numbers;
the reference configuration runs 512 slices at width 512, stated with the
commands in @sec-using-config.

```{python}
#| label: setup-arch
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize
```


```{python}
#| label: setup-arch-source
#| include: false
# Code listings are extracted from the class's source files by symbol name as the page renders, so they cannot drift
# from the code: a renamed function or a moved marker comment fails the render instead of printing stale code.
import ast, textwrap
from pathlib import Path
import physicsnemo
ISLA_SRC = Path(physicsnemo.__file__).parent / "experimental" / "models" / "isla"

def _symbol(tree, qualname):
    body, node = tree.body, None
    for part in qualname.split("."):
        node = next(n for n in body if isinstance(n, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef, ast.ClassDef)) and n.name == part)
        body = node.body
    return node

def listing(filename, qualname, start=None, end=None, docstring=False):
    """Print the source of `qualname` in `filename` as a fenced block; with `start`/`end`, only the lines of the
    function between the first line containing `start` and the next line containing `end` (end=None: to the end)."""
    src = (ISLA_SRC / filename).read_text(); lines = src.splitlines(); tree = ast.parse(src)
    node = _symbol(tree, qualname); a, b = node.lineno, node.end_lineno
    first = node.body[0]
    if not docstring and isinstance(first, ast.Expr) and isinstance(getattr(first, "value", None), ast.Constant) and isinstance(first.value.value, str):
        lines = lines[:first.lineno - 1] + lines[first.end_lineno:]; b -= first.end_lineno - first.lineno + 1
    block = lines[a - 1:b]
    where = f"{filename}: {qualname}"
    if start is not None:
        i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(block) if start in l)
        j = next(k for k, l in enumerate(block) if end in l and k > i) if end else len(block)
        block = block[i:j]; where += f", from the line containing `{start}`" + (f" to the one containing `{end}`" if end else " to the end")
    print(f"```python\n# {where}\n" + textwrap.dedent("\n".join(block)).rstrip() + "\n```")
```


## Notation {#sec-arch-notation}

**One symbol per quantity, one code name per symbol.** Indices: $i, j$ run
over the $N$ tokens, $s, t$ over the $M$ slices, $k$ over the $K$ global
vector inputs. Batch axes are omitted throughout. The code carries a
leading batch dimension on every tensor.

| symbol | shape | code | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x_i, n_i, w_i$ | $N{\times}3,\ N{\times}3,\ N$ | `cell_centroids`, `cell_normals`, `cell_measures` of the boundary meshes | sampled boundary positions, outward normals, the surface area each sample stands for (the cell's effective measure when the mesh carries one, else its geometric measure) |
| $g_k$, $\sigma$ | $K{\times}3$, $S$ | `global_schema` (rank 1, rank 0) | the problem's global directions and scalars, as named fields (external aerodynamics, the benchmark instance: $K = 1$, the far-field flow direction; $S = 0$ on the surface tasks, $S = 1$ on AirfRANS) |
| $v_{ip}$, $T_{iq}$ | $N{\times}P{\times}3$, $N{\times}Q{\times}3{\times}3$ | `boundary_schema`, `query_schema` (rank 1, rank 2) | per-token tensor inputs (a prescribed traction, a prescribed stress); $P = Q = 0$ on the aerodynamic tasks |
| $\hat g_k$, $\hat n_i$ | $K{\times}3$, $N{\times}3$ | `g_unit`, `n_hat` | the same directions and normals, normalized to unit length |
| $L$ | scalar | `gauge` | the length unit: the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample |
| $r_i$ | $N{\times}3$ | `r` | position in length units, $x_i / L$; used only inside differences |
| $\ell_i$ | $N$ | `log_w` | $\log w_i$, the measure bias of every routing softmax |
| $s_i$ | $N{\times}(K + n_b + S)$ | `invariants` | the seed: the scalars a token knows before any layer runs ($n_b$ counts the boundary inputs' invariants) |
| $h_i$ | $N{\times}d$ | `h` | the token state, width $d$ (`hidden`) |
| $\lambda_{is}$, $\lambda'_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `logits`, `logits + bias` | routing logits before and after the geometric refinement |
| $a_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `a` | routing weights: a softmax over tokens $i$ for each slice $s$ |
| $z_s, m_s$ | $M{\times}3$ | `z_pos`, `m_s` | the anchor of slice $s$: its mean position and mean normal direction |
| $\rho_{is}$, $\xi_{is}$ | $N{\times}M{\times}3$, $N{\times}M{\times}(5+K+P'+Q)$ | `rel`, `geo` | the token-to-anchor separation and the relational invariants formed from it ($P'$ counts the per-token vectors beyond the normal and the global directions, $Q$ the rank-2 inputs; both zero on the aerodynamic tasks) |
| $\pi_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `point_mix` | read-back weights: a softmax over slices $s$ for each token $i$ |
| $\bar\xi_i$, $\gamma_i$ | $N{\times}(5+K)$, $N{\times}d/2$ | `pooled`, `geo_pool` | the invariants pooled over slices, and their projection |
| $Z_s$ | $M{\times}d$ | `z` | the slice state |
| $b_i$ | $N{\times}d$ | `back` | the slice states read back to token $i$ |
| $\hat u_i$ | $N{\times}3$ | `r_hat` | the head's radial direction: from the token's own soft anchor to the token |
| $e_\theta, e_\phi$ | $N{\times}3$ | `spherical_basis` | the tangential complements of $\hat u_i$ against another direction |
| $c_i$, $T_i$ | $N{\times}n_c$, $N{\times}3^r$ per output | `coeffs`, `out[name]` | the head's invariant coefficients and the assembled output fields, one per declared name and rank ($m = 2K + 3$ true basis vectors; a vector costs $m$ coefficients, a symmetric rank-2 tensor $m(m+1)/2 + 1$) |

$\mathrm{LN}$ is LayerNorm over the width; $\mathrm{MLP}$ is Linear–GELU–Linear
with a hidden width of $4d$ (`mlp_ratio`); $W$ with a subscript is a learned
affine map. Definitions use $\equiv$.

## The pass in one picture {#sec-arch-picture}

**From the inputs to the last slice layer, the model computes only scalars
that are invariant under rotation, translation and uniform rescaling.
Vectors are rebuilt once, at the output.** @fig-isla-pass is the whole
surface model. The interior arrangements of @sec-arch-modes change which
tokens enter and which the head reads. They add no stage.

    LAYER --> HF --> BASIS --> OUT
    FR -. r_i, n̂_i, ĝ_k, ℓ_i to every layer .-> LAYER

## Stage 1: inputs and the frame {#sec-arch-frame}

**The frame has a length unit and no origin.** The model receives the
boundary as named meshes and reads the sampled boundary off their cells,
$x_i, n_i, w_i$ (centroid, normal, effective measure), together with the
global inputs $g_k$ and $\sigma$ (@sec-isla-inputs). It normalizes every
direction it is given,
$\hat g_k \equiv g_k / \lvert g_k \rvert$ and $\hat n_i \equiv n_i / \lvert
n_i \rvert$, so the magnitude of a global vector never enters. A magnitude
that matters is a global scalar. The one length unit is a normalized
two-point integral of the geometry, with $\tilde w_i \equiv w_i / \sum_j w_j$:

$$
L \equiv \Big( \sum_{i,j} \tilde w_i\, \tilde w_j\, \lvert x_i - x_j \rvert^2 \Big)^{1/2}
      = \Big( 2 \sum_i \tilde w_i\, \lvert x_i - \bar x \rvert^2 \Big)^{1/2},
\qquad
r_i \equiv x_i / L,
\qquad
\ell_i \equiv \log w_i .
$$

The code evaluates the second form (`rms_pairwise_distance`, in $O(N)$
through the variance identity). The weighted mean $\bar x$ is an
intermediate of this scalar only and is never used as a center. $L$ is
unchanged by a translation or rotation and scales with the geometry. It is
unchanged by a uniform rescale of the weights alone, because they are
normalized first, and it converges under refinement of any boundary whose
normalized measure converges (@sec-isla-frame). The scaled positions $r_i$
are never fed to a learned map. They enter only as differences $r_i - z_s$
in stage 3 and stage 4. The log measure $\ell_i$ is the bias that turns
every routing softmax into a quadrature rule (@sec-isla-quadrature). It is
always present: a boundary mesh without stored effective measures
contributes its cells' geometric measures.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Stage 1 in the code"}
The length unit is one function, and the frame is six lines of `_forward_tensors`: no center survives either.

## Stage 2: the seed and the embedding {#sec-arch-seed}

**A token's seed is every origin-free scalar the inputs offer, and it is
small.** With no origin, a position alone has no invariant. The only
scalars in $\{\hat n_i, \hat g_k\}$ that survive rotation are the cosines
between them. The seed is therefore

$$
s_i \equiv \big[\, \hat n_i \!\cdot\! \hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat n_i \!\cdot\! \hat g_K,\ \beta_i,\ \sigma \,\big]
\quad (K + n_b + S \text{ scalars}),
\qquad
h_i \equiv \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_i),
$$

where $\beta_i$ are the invariants of the optional per-cell boundary
inputs and $\sigma$ the global scalars, broadcast to every token. Of the
`boundary_schema` fields, a rank-0 field is its own scalar. A rank-1 field $v_i$
contributes $v_i \cdot \hat n_i$, $v_i \cdot \hat g_k$ and $\lvert v_i
\rvert$. A rank-2 field contributes its frame contractions, trace and
Frobenius norm (@sec-isla-inputs-rank). On the aerodynamic tasks of this
book $n_b = 0$, so on the surface tasks the seed is a single number per
token: the cosine between the normal and the far-field direction. If the
seed would be empty ($K = n_b = S = 0$), every token starts from one
learned constant. All separation between tokens then comes from the slice
layers, where a token learns where it sits relative to the anchors
(`_seed_invariants`, `embed`).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Stage 2 in the code"}
The seed is the cosines against the global directions, the boundary-input invariants and the global scalars, in that order; `_InputSet._features` is where a rank-1 or rank-2 per-token field becomes the invariants $\beta_i$ (@sec-isla-inputs-rank).

## Stage 3: the slice layer {#sec-arch-layer}

**A slice layer routes the tokens softly into $M$ slices, forms one anchor
per slice, describes every token relative to every anchor by invariant
scalars, and sends information up to the slices and back down together with
those scalars.** It is the one block that repeats, twelve times, each copy
with its own parameters (`_SliceBlock`). Its inputs are the token state
$h_i$ and the four frame quantities of stage 1, which every layer receives
unchanged: $r_i$, $\hat n_i$, $\hat g_k$, $\ell_i$. Its output is the
updated $h_i$. @fig-isla-layer shows the ten steps. The equations follow in
the same order.

%%|   routing (each slice's weights sum to one, with the measure bias) and over
%%|   slices for the read-back (each token's weights sum to one, without it).
%%|   How to read this: the only tensor that is $N{\times}M$ in the width of

**a. Routing logits.** A learned map of the normalized token state gives a
logit per token–slice pair (`_RoutingLogits`, @sec-isla-routing-forms): a
fixed temperature $T = 10$ (`ROUTING_TEMPERATURE`) times the cosine between
the normalized state and a prototype $p_s$ per slice. This bounds every
logit in $[-T, T]$:

$$
\tilde h_i \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
\lambda_{is} = T\, \frac{\tilde h_i \cdot p_s}{\lVert \tilde h_i \rVert\, \lVert p_s \rVert} .
$$

The prototypes are synthesized per sample from learned seeds $S_s$ and the
sample's own token states. Each seed attends over the tokens with a
measure-weighted softmax; the attended value term is centered across the
slices and passed through a smooth bound before it is added to the seed:

$$
\Delta_s = \sum_i \mathrm{softmax}_i\!\left(\tfrac{S_s \cdot k(\tilde h_i)}{\sqrt{H}} + \ell_i\right) v(\tilde h_i),
\qquad
\tilde\Delta_s = \Delta_s - \tfrac{1}{S}\textstyle\sum_{s'} \Delta_{s'},
\qquad
p_s = S_s + \frac{g\,\mathrm{rms}(S)}{\mathrm{rms}(\tilde\Delta) + g\,\mathrm{rms}(S)}\, \tilde\Delta_s ,
$$

with $k$ and $v$ linear maps, $g$ one learned scalar per block (initialized
at 0.1) and $\mathrm{rms}$ the root-mean-square entry of a matrix. Centering
removes the component common to every prototype, which carries no routing
information under a cosine and, when it dominates, folds every prototype
onto one direction; the bound holds the sample-dependent part to a fraction
$g$ of the seeds' spread, so a token cloud whose attention is the same for
every seed leaves the prototypes equal to the seeds. Token states are
invariant, so the prototypes are invariant and every contract holds
(`_RoutingLogits`). The bound on the logit, and what an unbounded affine
logit does without it, are in @sec-isla-routing-forms.

**b. Provisional routing.** A softmax over the *tokens*, for each slice,
with the measure bias:

$$
a^0_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)} .
$$

Each slice's weights sum to one over the tokens. Anything of the form
$\sum_i a^0_{is} f_i$ is therefore a measure-weighted mean of $f$ over the
slice, a quadrature estimate of a surface integral (`_softmax_over_points`).

**c. Anchors.** From those weights each slice forms its mean position and
its mean normal direction (`z_pos`, `m_s`):

$$
z_s \equiv \sum_i a^0_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
m_s \equiv \frac{\sum_i a^0_{is}\, \hat n_i}{\big\lvert \sum_i a^0_{is}\, \hat n_i \big\rvert} .
$$

Both are weighted sums of vectors that rotate with the body, with weights
that do not, so the anchors rotate and translate with the body
(@sec-isla-slices).

**d. Relational invariants.** For every token–anchor pair, with the
separation $\rho_{is} \equiv r_i - z_s$ and its direction $\hat\rho_{is}$,
the layer forms $5 + K$ scalars (`_relational_invariants`; drawn in
@fig-isla-relational):

$$
\xi_{is} \equiv \big[\,
\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\ \log\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat n_i,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\! m_s,\
\hat n_i\!\cdot\! m_s
\,\big] .
$$

Every entry is a norm or a dot product of vectors that move together, and
every position appears as a difference. No origin and no axis is referred
to (@sec-isla-relational). A model with rank-1 or rank-2 per-token inputs
appends more entries in the same place: $\hat\rho_{is} \cdot v$ for every
per-token vector $v$ (the inputs themselves and the vectors $T \hat n_i$,
$T \hat g_k$ derived from a rank-2 input $T$), and $\hat\rho_{is}^{\mathsf T}
T \hat\rho_{is}$ for every rank-2 input. The width is then $5 + K + P' + Q$
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank). On the aerodynamic tasks it is $5 + K$.

**e. Refinement, and the read-back weights.** A linear map of the
invariants to one scalar per pair refines the routing logit (`geo_logit`).
A slice can then prefer tokens near its anchor, along the global direction
from it, or facing it. The *same* refined logits, normalized over the
slices for each token and without the measure bias, are the read-back
weights (`point_mix`):

$$
\lambda'_{is} = \lambda_{is} + w_g \cdot \xi_{is} + b_g, \qquad
\pi_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda'_{it})} .
$$

**f. Routing.** The routing weights are recomputed from the refined logits
with the measure bias, exactly as in step b:

$$
a_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda'_{js} + \ell_j)} .
$$

@fig-isla-routing-readback shows the two normalizations side by side on the
airfoil: the same matrix of logits, read one way as "what each slice
averages" and the other way as "where each token reads from".

**g. Slice states.** Each slice aggregates the token states it routes, a
measure-weighted mean, and transforms the result with its own residual MLP
(`slice_mlp`):

$$
Z_s = \sum_i a_{is}\, h_i, \qquad
Z_s \leftarrow Z_s + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{slice}}(\mathrm{LN}(Z_s)) .
$$

In the surface configuration, this is the only place tokens exchange
information: through $M$ slice states (256 by default, 512 in the
reference configuration), never pairwise.

**h. Read-back.** Each token reads the slice states with its read-back
weights, and reads the invariants pooled with the same weights, projected
to half the width (`back`, `pooled`, `geo_feat`):

$$
b_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, Z_s, \qquad
\bar\xi_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, \xi_{is}, \qquad
\gamma_i = W_f\, \bar\xi_i + b_f .
$$

**i. Broadcast.** The token state, what it read, and where it sits are
combined by one affine map into a residual update (`broadcast`):

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + W_b\, [\, h_i;\ b_i;\ \gamma_i \,] .
$$

**j. Token MLP.** A pre-norm residual MLP closes the layer (`norm_mlp`,
`mlp`):

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_i)) .
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-routing-readback
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The two softmaxes of a slice layer, on the airfoil with six slices and
#|   eighty cells (the hand-made logits of @fig-isla-slices stand in for the
#|   learned ones; cells are finer near the leading edge). Top: the routing
#|   weights $a_{is}$, a softmax over tokens for each slice with the measure
#|   bias, so each row sums to one and a slice is a quadrature average of the
#|   cells it covers; the fine leading-edge cells receive individually smaller
#|   weights because they stand for less surface. Bottom: the read-back weights
#|   $\pi_{is}$, a softmax over slices for each token without the bias, so each
#|   column sums to one and a token chooses where to read. How to read this:
#|   both matrices come from the same logits; the model has 256 slices and
#|   200,000 tokens per case, so its matrices are much sparser than these.
#| code-fold: true
frac = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(1.0 - 0.6 * np.sin(np.linspace(0, np.pi, 80)) ** 4)]); frac /= frac[-1]
JJ = joukowski(n_cells=80, frac=frac)      # finer cells around the leading edge (mid-arclength)
s_arc = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); s_mid = (s_arc[:-1] + s_arc[1:]) / 2; total = s_arc[-1]
n_sl = 6
centers = (np.arange(n_sl) + 0.5) / n_sl * total
d = np.abs(s_mid[:, None] - centers[None, :]); d = np.minimum(d, total - d)
logits = -(d / (0.06 * total)) ** 2                       # (tokens, slices)
lw_ = np.log(JJ["w"])[:, None]
a = np.exp(logits + lw_); a /= a.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)    # softmax over tokens, per slice
pi = np.exp(logits); pi /= pi.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)        # softmax over slices, per token
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 4.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.35))
for ax, mat, title, vmax in ((axes[0], a.T, r"routing $a_{is}$: softmax over tokens, with the measure bias $\ell_i$; each row sums to 1", None),
                             (axes[1], pi.T, r"read-back $\pi_{is}$: softmax over slices, no bias; each column sums to 1", 1.0)):
    im = ax.imshow(mat, aspect="auto", cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax if vmax else mat.max(), interpolation="nearest")
    ax.grid(False); ax.set_yticks(range(n_sl)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"slice {k + 1}" for k in range(n_sl)], fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5, loc="left", color=INK)
    for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_visible(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
    cb.set_label("weight [–]", fontsize=8.5)
i_le = int(np.argmin(JJ["mid"][:, 0]))
axes[1].set_xlabel("token $i$ along the surface, from the trailing edge around the leading edge and back [index]", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(i_le, color=WHITE, lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[1].text(i_le + 0.8, n_sl - 0.55, "leading edge", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=WHITE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Two identities the implementation relies on"}
**Pool first, then project.** The invariants $\xi_{is}$ are $N{\times}M{\times}(5+K)$.
Projecting each pair to width $d/2$ and then pooling would make autograd
store an $N{\times}M{\times}d/2$ tensor per layer. The projection is affine
and $\pi_{is}$ sums to one over slices, so
$\sum_s \pi_{is}(W_f \xi_{is} + b_f) = W_f \sum_s \pi_{is} \xi_{is} + b_f$.
The code therefore pools first and saves only $N{\times}(5+K)$. The
identity is tested at $10^{-12}$ (@sec-isla-contracts).

**Rebuild the geometry in the backward pass.** Steps c to e and the pooling
of step h are one *geometry region* per layer (`_geo_region`): a function
of $(\lambda, r, \hat n, \hat g, z, m)$ with no parameters but $w_g, b_g$.
On the eager path, `geo_checkpoint=True` recomputes its $N{\times}M{\times}\cdot$
intermediates in the backward pass instead of storing them, with
bitwise-identical outputs and gradients. The fused Triton kernel
(`geo_kernel="fused"`, the automatic choice on CUDA with one to four
per-point vectors, at most 1,024 slices and no rank-2 per-token input)
evaluates the same region without ever materializing them, with the
recompute built in (@sec-using-cost).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Stage 3 in the code"}
One slice block's forward is steps a to j in order; `_RoutingLogits` is step a with the prototype synthesis, and `_relational_invariants` is step d on the eager path (the fused kernel computes the same scalars without materializing them).

## Stage 4: the head frame {#sec-arch-head-frame}

**The vector head needs one direction per token that points from the body
to the token, and ISLA takes it from the token's own soft anchor, not from
a center.** After the last layer, one more routing map (`frame_assign`,
acting on the final $h_i$) gives logits $\lambda^f_{is}$. Read one way they
give anchors, read the other way they give each token's soft assignment:

$$
a^f_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda^f_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda^f_{js} + \ell_j)}, \qquad
z^f_s = \sum_i a^f_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
\beta_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda^f_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda^f_{it})}, \qquad
u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is}\, z^f_s, \qquad
\hat u_i = u_i / \lvert u_i \rvert .
$$

$u_i$ is a difference of positions, so $\hat u_i$ rotates with the body and
is unchanged by a translation. No centroid appears (`a_f`, `z_f`, `b_f`,
`r_hat`; the construction is @fig-isla-basis).

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Stage 4 in the code"}
The head frame is the tail of `_forward_tensors`: one more routing map, read both ways, and a difference of positions.

```{python}

#| output: asis
listing("model.py", "ISLA._forward_tensors", start="### Head frame:", end="### The token basis.")
```
:::

## Stage 5: the head {#sec-arch-head}

**One linear head produces every output's invariant coefficients, and each
output of declared rank $r$ is contracted from them over tensor products of
$r$ vectors the token already has.** On the normalized final state
(`norm_out`, `head`):

$$
c_i = W_h\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i) + b_h, \qquad c_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c},
$$

with $n_c$ the sum over the declared outputs of their coefficient counts.
The true basis at token $i$, in the order the code stacks it, is

$$
t_i = \big\{\, \hat g_1, \dots, \hat g_K,\ \hat n_i,\ \hat u_i,\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\ e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_1),\ \dots \,\big\}
\quad (m = 2K + 3 \text{ vectors}),
$$

with the tangential complement of $\hat u$ against a second direction
$\hat a$ defined, unnormalized, as

$$
e_\theta(\hat u, \hat a) \equiv -\hat a + (\hat a \cdot \hat u)\, \hat u
$$

(`spherical_basis` with `normalize_basis_vectors=False`). It vanishes
smoothly where $\hat u \parallel \hat a$, which is why it is left
unnormalized. The pseudovector basis is the set of cross products of the
primaries $\{\hat g_k, \hat n_i, \hat u_i\}$ ($p = \binom{K+2}{2}$
vectors). An output declared with rank $r$ and even parity is

$$
T_i = \sum_{j_1 \dots j_r} c_{i\, j_1 \dots j_r}\; t_{i j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes t_{i j_r}
\;+\; \sum_k c_{ik}^{\mathrm{iso}}\, I_k ,
$$

where the isotropic tensors $I_k$ are the identity at rank 2 and the three
products of Kronecker deltas at rank 4 (their symmetric sum for a symmetric
spec). A symmetric spec carries one coefficient per unordered multi-index.
An odd-parity spec replaces exactly one factor by a pseudovector, with the
Levi-Civita symbol as the isotropic term at rank 3. The code gathers the
free coefficients into the full coefficient tensor over ordered
multi-indices and contracts one index at a time, so the basis of $m^r$
products is never materialized (`_OutputLayout`, `_assemble_output`). The
coefficient counts per output are $1$ at rank 0, $m$ at rank 1 ($5$ with
one global direction), $m^2 + 1$ or $m(m+1)/2 + 1$ (symmetric) at rank 2
($26$ or $16$), $m^3$ or $\binom{m+2}{3}$ at rank 3, and $m^4 + 3$ or
$\binom{m+3}{4} + 1$ at rank 4. The class refuses ranks above 4. The model
returns a point-cloud `Mesh` whose `points` are the prediction points (the
boundary token positions on a surface task) and whose `point_data` holds
one leaf per declared output name. In every surface result of the book
these are pressure, a rank-0 field of shape $N$, and wall shear stress, a
rank-1 field of shape $N{\times}3$. Under an orthogonal map $R$
every true basis vector maps as $R t$, every pseudovector as $\det(R)\, R t$,
and every coefficient is unchanged. An even output therefore maps as
$R^{\otimes r} T$ and an odd one as $\det(R)\, R^{\otimes r} T$. That is the
covariance proof, for rotations and reflections alike, and
@sec-isla-contracts lists the tests that check it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Stage 5 in the code"}
The basis is stacked in the order the text gives, and each declared output is contracted from its coefficients one index at a time.

## Where the parameters are {#sec-arch-params}

**Almost all of ISLA's parameters are ordinary MLPs. The geometry costs
seven numbers per layer.** @tbl-isla-params counts them from the class at
two widths, 12 layers and 256 slices.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-isla-params
#| output: asis
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import torch
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA
cnt = lambda mod: sum(p.numel() for p in mod.parameters())
widths = (192, 384)
models = {w: ISLA(output_schema={"pressure": {"rank": 0}, "wss": {"rank": 1}}, global_schema={"freestream": {"rank": 1}}, hidden=w, n_layers=12, n_slices=256) for w in widths}
def rows_for(m):
    blk = m.blocks[0]
    return [
        ("embedding MLP (stage 2)", "`embed`", cnt(m.embed), 1),
        ("routing map, with its LayerNorm (step a)", "`norm_assign`, `assign`", cnt(blk.norm_assign) + cnt(blk.assign), 12),
        ("routing refinement (step e)", "`geo_logit`", cnt(blk.geo_logit), 12),
        ("pooled-invariant projection (step h)", "`geo_feat`", cnt(blk.geo_feat), 12),
        ("slice MLP, with its LayerNorm (step g)", "`slice_mlp`", cnt(blk.slice_mlp), 12),
        ("broadcast (step i)", "`broadcast`", cnt(blk.broadcast), 12),
        ("token MLP, with its LayerNorm (step j)", "`norm_mlp`, `mlp`", cnt(blk.norm_mlp) + cnt(blk.mlp), 12),
        ("head-frame routing map (stage 4)", "`frame_assign`", cnt(m.frame_assign), 1),
        ("head, with its LayerNorm (stage 5)", "`norm_out`, `head`", cnt(m.norm_out) + cnt(m.head), 1),
    ]
R = {w: rows_for(models[w]) for w in widths}
totals = {w: cnt(models[w]) for w in widths}
for w in widths:
    assert sum(c * n for _, _, c, n in R[w]) == totals[w]
out = "| component | code | copies | parameters in all, 192 wide | share | parameters in all, 384 wide | share |\n|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for (name, code, c192, n), (_, _, c384, _) in zip(R[192], R[384]):
    out += (f"| {name} | {code} | {n} | {c192 * n:,} | {100 * c192 * n / totals[192]:.1f}% "
            f"| {c384 * n:,} | {100 * c384 * n / totals[384]:.1f}% |\n")
out += f"| **total** | | | **{totals[192]:,}** | 100% | **{totals[384]:,}** | 100% |\n"
out += ("\n: Parameter count of ISLA at 12 layers, 256 slices, one scalar and one vector output and one global vector input, at width 192 "
        "and at width 384 (the ladders' width; the reference configuration and the class default are 512 wide with 512 slices), computed from the class as the page renders. How to read this: the shares barely move with width because every large component is "
        "quadratic in it; the routing maps and the geometry are the exceptions. {#tbl-isla-params}\n")
print(out)
```

The two per-layer MLPs hold most of the total. The broadcast maps and the
routing maps (the $M \times d$ seeds plus the $2d^2$ key and value maps of
the prototype synthesis, per block) hold most of the rest. Width $d$
therefore sets the count quadratically and the slice count $M$ linearly.
That is why the capacity ladders of @sec-equal-budget move width and not
slices.

## The two tasks: surface and interior {#sec-arch-modes}

**The surface task and the interior task share the five stages. They
differ in which points are tokens and which the head reads, and the choice
is made at construction (`interior=False` or `True`).** @fig-isla-modes
places them side by side. Everything above described the first. Every
interior result of the book uses the second. The two own different
parameter sets (the interior task adds the prediction-point embedding, type
offset and routing mass), which is why the task is a constructor argument:
a parameter that takes no part in a forward pass stops distributed
training.

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   The two tasks of ISLA. Surface: the boundary cells are the tokens and
%%|   the head reads every one of them. Interior: the prediction points join
%%|   the encoder as interacting tokens with a learned routing mass, and the
%%|   head reads them alone (the configuration the interior results of the
%%|   book use). How to read this: the slice layer, head frame and head are
%%|   the same modules in both; only the token set and which tokens the head
%%|   reads change.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef aqua fill:#e3f6ef,stroke:#1baf7a,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph S["surface task (interior=False, the default)"]
        direction TB
        S1["boundary tokens (N)"]:::data
        S2["slice layers × 12"]:::learned
        S3["head frame + head on all N tokens"]:::learned
        S1 --> S2 --> S3
    end
    subgraph Q["interior task (interior=True): prediction points as tokens"]
        direction TB
        Q1["boundary tokens (N)"]:::data
        Q2["prediction-point tokens (Q): position and declared query inputs; direction and signed distance<br/>to the nearest boundary sample computed inside; learned routing mass"]:::aqua
        Q3["slice layers × 12 on all N + Q tokens"]:::learned
        Q4["head frame + head on the Q query tokens"]:::learned
        Q1 --> Q3
        Q2 --> Q3 --> Q4
    end
```

**Prediction points as tokens** (`interior=True`;
@sec-interior-query-tokens). Each prediction point $q$ arrives as a
position $x_q$ (the `points` of the prediction `Mesh`, or a bare
$Q{\times}3$ tensor) and whatever per-point fields were declared in
`query_schema` (from its `point_data`). Its invariants need two more
quantities: a direction to stand in for the normal, and a distance to the
wall. Both are functions of the boundary sample and of $x_q$, and the model
always computes them itself; they are never inputs. With $i^* \equiv
\arg\min_i \lvert x_q - x_i \rvert$ the nearest boundary sample,

$$
\hat n_q \equiv \frac{x_q - x_{i^*}}{\lvert x_q - x_{i^*} \rvert}, \qquad
\delta_q \equiv \operatorname{sign}\big(\hat n_q \cdot \hat n_{i^*}\big)\, \lvert x_q - x_{i^*} \rvert ,
$$

are the direction from the boundary to the query and the distance signed by
the nearest sample's normal. The distance is positive on the side the
normal points to (outside, for outward normals). A query on a sample takes
that sample's normal and $\delta_q = 0$. Both are differences of positions,
so the distance is invariant and the direction covariant under every rigid
motion and reflection, and the distance scales with the geometry. The
search is exact and goes through the project's shared nearest-neighbour
routine (`physicsnemo.nn.functional.neighbors.knn.knn`, cuML on CUDA and a
SciPy KD-tree on the host), so the $Q \times N$ distance matrix is never
held at once (`nearest_boundary_geometry`). The point is then placed in
the same frame and seeded like a boundary cell, with zeros in the
boundary-input channels. It receives a learned type offset and an
embedding of the distance in frame units followed by the declared query
inputs (rank-0 entries divided by $L$ and paired with a signed log, rank-1
and rank-2 entries through their invariants, @sec-isla-inputs-rank):

$$
r_q = x_q / L, \qquad
h_q = \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_q) + t_{\mathrm{q}}
      + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{qs}}\!\big(\,[\, \delta_q / L,\ \operatorname{sign}(\delta_q) \log(\lvert \delta_q \rvert / L + \epsilon),\ \text{declared query inputs} \,]\big) .
$$

The distance is to the *sampled* boundary, 200,000 of up to 17 million
cells on a DrivAerML car. Near the wall it therefore overestimates the true
wall distance by up to about the sample spacing, and the direction deviates
from the true gradient of the signed-distance field by the same order. Far
from the wall both agree with the full-resolution field. A dataset that
stores a full-mesh signed-distance field and its gradient passes them as
ordinary `query_schema` fields (a rank-0 and a rank-1 field, like any
other PDE datum); the model's own geometry is computed regardless. Every
interior lane of this book passes the stored field as well
(@sec-interior-query-tokens).

A prediction point's measure bias is not an area but a learned share of
the boundary's total measure, split equally over the $Q$ points:

$$
\ell_q = \omega + \log \sum_{i \le N} w_i - \log Q ,
$$

Re-representing the same surface on finer cells therefore changes nothing
(`test_query_mass_refinement_invariance`), and rescaling the geometry
shifts every token's bias by the same amount. The $N + Q$ tokens then run
through the twelve slice layers together. The head frame builds its
anchors from all of them, and the head reads the $Q$ prediction-point
tokens only. The arrangement is exactly covariant and not
query-independent (@sec-isla-contracts).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The interior task in the code"}
The prediction points' geometry is one function on the boundary sample, and the tokens are appended before the slice layers run.

### The read-only interior task {#sec-arch-passive-decoder}

**With `query_independent=True` the prediction points are passive: at
every slice layer they read the slices the boundary formed at that layer
and never write into them, so the prediction at a point is a function of
that point and the boundary alone.** A passive point is seeded and
embedded as an interacting one is (the built-in direction and signed
distance, the declared query inputs, the type offset) and runs through
the same twelve slice layers with the same parameters as the boundary
tokens. Only its measure bias differs: $\ell_q = -\infty$ in place of the
learned routing mass, so every softmax over tokens gives it zero weight.
It takes no part in the routing prototypes, the anchors $z_s, m_s$ (step
c), the routing weights $a_{is}$ (step f), the slice states $Z_s$ (step
g) or the head frame's anchors (stage 4). It still forms its own logits,
its relational invariants against the anchors and its read-back weights
$\pi_{qs}$, and it reads $b_q = \sum_s \pi_{qs} Z_s$ (step h). The
boundary tokens therefore compute what they compute in the surface task
whatever points are requested, and a request split into chunks,
permuted, or reduced to one point returns the same predictions to
$10^{-12}$ in float64 (`test_query_independent_interior_contracts`). This
mode has no routing-mass parameter. The interacting task is the class
default and the configuration of every interior standing in the book.
Its dependence on the request is measured in @sec-interior-companion.

A passive point reads at matched depth: at layer $\ell$ it reads the
slices formed from the boundary states at layer $\ell$, the depth its own
state has reached. That alignment carries much of the read-only model's
accuracy. A control with the same parameters, in which the boundary first
runs through all twelve layers and every layer's points then read slices
formed from that final boundary state, has 1.37 to 1.40 times the
matched-depth model's error on the DrivAerML Volume task and 1.56 to 1.72
times on the AirfRANS interior task. Doubling the slice count changes
neither the read-only nor the interacting model beyond seed noise
(@tbl-arch-read-depth).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Matched depth and slice count, measured"}
| model | DrivAerML Volume: p / v / nut | ÷ its base | AirfRANS: p / v / nut | ÷ its base |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| passive points, matched depth (base) | 0.0449 / 0.0834 / 0.147 | 1 | 0.0328 / 0.0180 / 0.0346 | 1 |
| passive points reading the final boundary state | 0.0615 / 0.1147 / 0.206 | 1.37 / 1.38 / 1.40 | 0.0522 / 0.0281 / 0.0596 | 1.59 / 1.56 / 1.72 |
| passive points, twice the slices | 0.0449 / 0.0829 / 0.152 | 1.00 / 0.99 / 1.04 | 0.0370 / 0.0181 / 0.0351 | 1.13 / 1.01 / 1.01 |
| interacting points (base) | 0.0394 / 0.0635 / 0.0876 | 1 | 0.0350 / 0.0170 / 0.0314 | 1 |
| interacting points, twice the slices | 0.0391 / 0.0626 / 0.0864 | 0.99 / 0.99 / 0.99 | 0.0351 / 0.0171 / 0.0313 | 1.00 / 1.00 / 1.00 |

: Matched-depth reading and slice count: relative L2 of interior pressure / velocity / eddy viscosity (p / v / nut), float32, seed means of two seeds (42, 43), 500 epochs, no boundary read in any row. DrivAerML Volume task: 435 training cars, 48 validation cars, 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000 interior points per car, ISLA width 512, 12 layers, 512 slices (1,024 when doubled), learning rate 3.75e-4. AirfRANS interior task: 800 training airfoils, 200 test airfoils, 100,000 interior points (one contiguous window of the stored points, so the ratios compare like with like and the absolute errors do not carry over; @sec-interior-airfrans) and the whole airfoil polyline, ISLA at 384 wide, 12 layers, 256 slices (512 when doubled), 5e-4 (the earlier ISLA reference). #### The global boundary read {#sec-arch-global-read}

**A passive point can also read the boundary cells themselves: with
`kernel_read="mean"` and `kernel_read_radius=None`, after every slice
layer each prediction point adds a measure-weighted average of the cells'
states over the whole boundary, weighted by a learned kernel of where
each cell sits relative to the point and by how well their states
match.** For a point $q$ and a cell $j$, with $\rho_{qj} \equiv r_q -
r_j$, the kernel sees the pair's invariants $\iota_{qj}$: the distance
$\lvert\rho_{qj}\rvert$, its logarithm, $\log(\lvert\rho_{qj}\rvert /
\lvert\delta_q\rvert)$ (the distance in units of the point's own wall
distance), the cosines of $\hat\rho_{qj}$ with $\hat n_j$, $\hat n_q$ and
every $\hat g_k$, and $\hat n_q \cdot \hat n_j$ and $\hat n_j \cdot \hat
g_k$ (declared per-token vectors add their own cosines). One MLP shared
by every layer maps $\iota_{qj}$ to 16 basis functions per pair, once per
forward pass, and each layer's kernel $\kappa_h$ is a learned combination
of them for each of 8 heads. With $\omega_j \equiv w_j / \sum_i w_i$ the
cell's share of the boundary measure, $\tilde h \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h)$
(one norm for cells, one for points) and $c = 4$ key channels per head,
the read after a layer is

$$
\alpha_{qjh} = \operatorname*{softmax}_j \Big( \kappa_h(\iota_{qj})
  + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{c}} \big\langle W^{\mathrm q}_h \tilde h_q,\ W^{\mathrm k}_h \tilde h_j \big\rangle
  + \log \omega_j \Big),
\qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W^{\mathrm o} \Big[ \textstyle\sum_j \alpha_{qjh}\, W^{\mathrm v}_h \tilde h_j \Big]_{h=1}^{8} ,
$$

where the brackets concatenate the heads' 8 value channels each and
$W^{\mathrm o}$ starts at zero, so training begins from the model without
the read. The log measure fraction makes the read a quadrature
(@sec-isla-quadrature): with the kernel and key terms constant it is the
measure-weighted mean of the cells' values, and splitting a cell into two
coincident halves or rescaling every measure changes nothing
(`test_tree_read_similarity_refinement_and_measure_scale_at_theta_zero`).
Every input is an invariant, so the read keeps the contracts of
@sec-isla-contracts, and it leaves the boundary tokens and the slices
untouched, so it keeps query independence
(`test_global_read_is_exactly_query_independent`). Evaluated pair by pair
it costs $Q \times N$ pairs per layer: $10^8$ for 100,000 points around a
1,000-segment airfoil, $4 \times 10^{10}$ for 200,000 points around a
200,000-cell car.

#### The read through a cluster forest {#sec-arch-tree-read}

**With `kernel_read_theta` set to a number $\theta$, the same read runs
through a Barnes-Hut forest: a point reads nearby cells one by one and
each distant cluster of similarly oriented cells as one virtual cell,
which takes a 200,000-cell car from $4 \times 10^{10}$ pairs per layer to
$1.6 \times 10^8$ at $\theta = 1$, keeps the prediction exactly query
independent and keeps it pose invariant up to ties of the boundary's own
frame.** ISLA-DTT is ISLA with passive prediction points, the global read
after every layer and the forest at $\theta = 1$. It is the one read-only
configuration the book scores (@sec-interior-read-only,
@sec-airfrans-read-only). The forest is built once per case, without
gradient:

1. The frame is the boundary's own: the principal axes of the cells'
   measure-weighted position covariance, each signed so that the third
   moment of the positions along it is positive. The forest is built in
   these coordinates, so it moves with the body.
2. The cells are split by the sign octant of their normal in that frame,
   and one cluster tree is built per octant
   (`physicsnemo.mesh.spatial.ClusterTree`, which bisects the boxes of a
   Morton space-filling curve down to leaves of 4 cells). Opposite normals
   never share a tree, so no cluster spans both faces of a thin body.
3. Every node carries a virtual cell: its cells' measure-weighted
   centroid, their renormalized measure-weighted mean normal, their mean
   rank-1 inputs and their total measure, and at every layer the
   measure-weighted means of their keys and values.
4. Each point walks every tree once. A node is read as one virtual cell
   when its box diagonal is below $\theta$ times the distance from the
   point to the box and its normals are coherent, the length of their
   mean exceeding $1 - \theta^2/2$ (their measure-weighted RMS chord about
   the mean is below $\theta$). A leaf that fails either test is read cell
   by cell, and any other node hands the point to its two children, so
   every cell is read exactly once, alone or inside one virtual cell
   (`test_point_pairs_admit_only_separated_coherent_nodes_and_cover_every_cell`).

The softmax of the global read then runs over the point's list, a virtual
cell entering with its total measure fraction as its log bias and its
invariants computed from its centroid and normal. Because the read is a
quadrature, a virtual cell is its cluster's monopole: were the logit
constant over the cluster, reading the virtual cell would equal reading
its cells one by one. The softmax of each point runs in a fused Triton
kernel that keeps nothing per pair between the forward and backward
passes.

Three properties hold by construction. At $\theta = 0$ no cluster is
admitted and the read is the dense read pair for pair, with the same
parameters (`test_tree_read_at_theta_zero_is_the_dense_read`). At every
$\theta$ a point's list depends on the forest and the point alone, so the
prediction is query independent
(`test_tree_read_is_exactly_query_independent_at_every_theta`). And a
rotation, reflection or translation of the case gives the same forest and
the same lists
(`test_forest_and_every_list_are_the_same_in_every_pose_at_finite_theta`),
up to ties of the boundary's frame: two equal principal variances, or an
axis without a third moment, whose sign then follows the laboratory axis
it overlaps most. On both interior datasets ISLA-DTT's error on rotated
and translated cases is its native error to the fourth digit on pressure
and velocity and within 0.3% on eddy viscosity. $\theta$ is a constant of
the trained model, like a kernel radius: ISLA-DTT trains and is scored at
$\theta = 1$, so its kernel, keys and values are learned as the forest
groups the cells.

On one GB300 at 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000 prediction points
(width 512, 512 slices, bfloat16, compiled slice layers, one forward and
backward pass), a point at $\theta = 1$ reads about 800 sources, 95% of
them virtual cells: $1.6 \times 10^8$ pairs per layer, 250 times fewer
than the dense read. The step takes 1.76 s and 194.5 GiB against 0.475 s
and 126 GiB for the same model without the boundary read, 3.7 times the
step. At $\theta = 0.5$ a point's list grows to about 6,900 sources, more
than one GB300 holds at this size. The read adds about 1.2 million
parameters to ISLA's 69 million. In training on AeroZoo, an interior-task
dataset of 3,816 cases with 200,000 interior points and up to 50,000
boundary faces per boundary type per case, on four GB300 ranks in
bfloat16 (the final epoch's median step), ISLA-DTT steps in 1.26 s with
162 GB on its busiest rank against ISLA's 0.68 s and 130 GB, 1.9 times
the step, at 70.3 million parameters against 69.1 million
(results/campaigns_2026-10-09/aerozoo/aerozoo_reduction.json, `cost`).

## What the pass never does {#sec-arch-never}

**The contracts of @sec-isla-contracts are absences, and two of them can be
read off the stages directly.**

- **No coordinate reaches a learned map, and no center is estimated.**
  $r_i$ enters only as $r_i - z_s$ (step d), $r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z^f_s$
  (stage 4) and $x_q - x_{i^*}$ (the interior geometry). Every learned
  input is a norm, a dot product, a log of one of those, or a supplied
  scalar. The one mean position computed, inside $L$, is consumed by a
  scalar. Anchors are means over *slices*, not over the body, and only
  their differences from tokens are used.
- **No positional encoding, and no prediction point attends to another.**
  Tokens exchange information through the $M$ slice states, and the
  routing that decides which slice a token joins is a function of the
  token's state and its relation to the anchors. The one pairwise read in
  the class is the global boundary read of the read-only task
  (@sec-arch-global-read): a passive prediction point attends to boundary
  cells, and nothing flows from it to any token.

## The switches {#sec-arch-switches}

**The class has one frame, one routing form, one length unit, and a small
set of arguments: the sizes, the declarations, the task and the role of
its prediction points, the read-only task's boundary read, three cost
knobs, the routing-prototype choice and the spatial dimension. Each row below
names the stage an argument touches.** Every argument is keyword-only. Anything else
that was once configurable has been fixed or deleted (the option policy is
stated in @sec-using-config); the fixed behaviour is described in the stages
above.

| argument (default) | stage | what it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `hidden` (512), `n_layers` (12), `n_slices` (512), `mlp_ratio` (4); the class defaults, which are the reference configuration (@sec-using-config) | all | $d$, the number of slice layers, $M$, and the MLP expansion |
| `output_schema` (required) | 5 | the output fields by name and rank spec (`{pressure: {rank: 0}, wss: {rank: 1}, stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}}`; `parity: odd` for a pseudotensor); each field costs the coefficient count of @sec-arch-head and is returned as a leaf of the output Mesh's `point_data` under its name. A dotted name (`surface.pressure`) is a nested leaf of the output and, in any input mapping, of the input; every declared value is a `{rank: ...}` spec or a nested group (a mapping of mappings), and several independent scalars are several rank-0 names |
| `global_schema` (none) | 1, 2, 3d, 5 | the per-case fields by name and rank, read from `global_data`: each rank-1 field is a global direction $\hat g_k$ (one seed cosine, one relational cosine, two basis vectors); each rank-0 field widens the seed |
| `boundary_schema` (none) | 2, 3d | per-cell fields by name and rank 0 to 2, read from every boundary mesh's `cell_data`: their invariants $\beta_i$ join the seed (prediction-point tokens carry zeros), and rank-1 and rank-2 fields add their contractions with $\hat\rho_{is}$ to the relational invariants (@sec-isla-inputs-rank) |
| `query_schema` (none) | interior | per-prediction-point fields by name and rank 0 to 2 (a material label, a source term, a stored signed distance and its gradient), read from the prediction Mesh's `point_data` and carried by the prediction-point tokens through their own embedding after the built-in distance channel; rank-0 fields are divided by $L$ and paired with a signed log |
| `interior` (`False`) | modes | the task: `False` predicts at the boundary cells and takes no prediction points; `True` predicts at the prediction points, which join the encoder as interacting tokens with the built-in nearest-boundary direction and signed distance (@sec-arch-modes) |
| `query_independent` (`False`) | modes | interior task only: `True` makes the prediction points passive (@sec-arch-passive-decoder), with no routing weight and no routing-mass parameter, so each prediction depends on its own point and the boundary alone |
| `kernel_read` (`None`), `kernel_read_radius` (0.01), `kernel_read_blocks` (`None`) | after each slice layer | read-only interior task only: `kernel_read="mean"` with `kernel_read_radius=None` adds the global boundary read after each of the last `kernel_read_blocks` layers, every layer when `None` (@sec-arch-global-read). A finite radius limits the read to the cells within that distance in units of $L$, and `"sum"` replaces the softmax by an unnormalized quadrature; neither is part of any configuration the book scores |
| `kernel_read_theta` (`None`) | after each slice layer | global read only: `None` evaluates it pair by pair, $Q \times N$ pairs per layer; a number $\theta$ evaluates it through the cluster forest at that opening angle (@sec-arch-tree-read), the dense read at 0. ISLA-DTT sets 1 and is trained at it |
| `geo_kernel` (`None`, automatic), `geo_checkpoint` (off) | 3c–3e, 3h | how the geometry region is executed: `None` resolves at the first forward pass to `"fused"` (the Triton kernel) when the inputs are on CUDA, Triton is importable, the global directions and rank-1 per-token inputs together number one to four, there are at most 1,024 slices and no rank-2 per-token input, and to `"eager"` (the PyTorch region) otherwise; either name forces that path, and `"fused"` raises where its constraints fail. `geo_checkpoint` rebuilds the eager region in backward instead of storing it. Neither changes the function computed beyond roundoff |
| `compile_blocks` (`False`) | 3 | each slice block's forward is wrapped in `torch.compile`, built lazily at the first call. Parameter names, the state dict and the eager path are unchanged, and the fused geometry kernel stays a custom-op leaf. Measured on four GB300 ranks at 200,000 cells per case: the DrivAerML Surface step falls from 221 to 180 ms and peak memory from 44.9 to 32.9 GiB, the Volume step from 475 to 308 ms and 88.5 to 64.5 GiB, with losses at bfloat16 roundoff. The recipe's ISLA configurations set it true |
| `dim` (3) | all | the spatial dimension: every boundary mesh is a `Mesh[dim - 1, dim]` (a polyline in two dimensions), every prediction point has `dim` coordinates, and the head's basis follows it (perpendiculars instead of cross products in two dimensions; odd-parity outputs refused for `dim >= 4`). The fused kernels are written for three dimensions; other dimensions run the eager region and the host nearest-neighbour search. A planar problem is passed with `dim=2`, never embedded with a zero third coordinate |
| `eps` ($10^{-12}$) | 1, 3c, 3d, 4 | the floor under every norm and logarithm |
